notes.meaning: Sailors heading home from distant ports receive tragic news when they stop at Cyprus. Tyre, the famous center of sea trade, has been crushed and its harbor wrecked. With no homes or docks left standing, the returning ships have nowhere to go.

The people along the coast and the traders of Sidon are told to fall silent in shock. Tyre was once filled with busy sailors and rich goods from across the sea. Now the lively trading has stopped, leaving only stunned silence.

Tyre built its great wealth by shipping crops across the Mediterranean from Egypt. The rich harvest grown along the Nile River was Tyre's main business, turning the city into the chief marketplace for the ancient world.

The older Phoenician city of Sidon is told to feel deep shame over what happened to Tyre. The fallen island fortress weeps like a mother who has lost all her children. All her bustling people and colonies are gone, as though she had never raised a family at all.
The news of Tyre's ruin will cause great fear and grief in Egypt. Egypt depended on Tyre's ships to export its grain, and Tyre served as a protective shield against northern empires.
The survivors are told to flee across the sea to distant colonies like Tarshish. They used to sail there as proud and wealthy traders, but now they must travel as weeping refugees looking for safety.

The prophet asks if this heap of ruins is really the joyful city that boasted of its ancient roots. Tyre was famous for sending its people across the sea to build colonies. Now its citizens are forced to walk far away as poor captives and exiles.

A question is raised about who could bring down such a majestic city. Tyre had the power to establish royal colonies and give out crowns, while its merchants were treated like princes across the known world.

The Lord of hosts planned this judgment Himself. He decided to shatter Tyre's boastful pride and bring down everyone who felt self-sufficient in earthly wealth. True security belongs to God, not human riches.

The distant colony of Tarshish is told to spread out freely across its own land like the overflowing Nile River. Tyre's tight grip and heavy demands have been broken, leaving the colony free from its old ruler.

The Lord stretched out His powerful hand over the sea and made nearby kingdoms shake with fear. He issued the command to tear down the coastal fortresses of Canaan. Even the strongest ocean defense cannot resist God's decree.
Tyre was once safe like an untouched daughter, but its celebration is over. The survivors are warned that even if they escape across the water to Cyprus, the reach of their enemies will follow them.

Isaiah points to Babylon as a warning example for Tyre. Babylon seemed weak at first and later built up palaces and towers, yet Assyrian forces battered it down into ruins. If a land as mighty as Babylon could be crushed, Tyre cannot hope to escape.
The merchant ships of Tarshish are called to weep again as the warning closes. The strong harbor that kept their ships safe and made them wealthy has been completely ruined.

Tyre will sit deserted and ignored for seventy years, matching the length of a kingdom's rule. When that long period ends, the city will begin trying to revive its old business, like an old song about a forgotten woman trying to regain attention.

Tyre is pictured as a neglected singer taking up a harp to walk through the streets. She plays sweet tunes and sings lively songs so people will notice her again. This describes how Tyre would use every tempting commercial skill to win back foreign business.
When the seventy years end, the Lord will step in with mercy to let Tyre recover. The city will quickly return to its old habits, dealing eagerly with every nation on earth for the sake of profit.

A time will come when the profits of Tyre will be dedicated to the Lord rather than locked away in selfish greed. Those earnings will be used to supply God's worshippers and ministers with plenty of food and durable clothing. This was seen when people from Tyre came to faith in Christ and shared their goods to support the early church.
